AbstractText.Label: PURPOSE
AbstractText.content: To investigate the effects of a community-based adapted walking intervention on a child with Pitt Hopkins syndrome (PTHS).

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: A four-year old boy with PTHS participated in a 12-week intervention comprising five one-hour long walking sessions per week at a local daycare. Walking sessions used the Upsee mobility device (Firefly by Leckey Ltd., Ireland). Outcome measures included Goal Attainment Scaling and the Mobility Ability Participation Assessment.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Parental and caregiver goals for social interaction, physical activity and physical health surpassed expectations by post-testing. Gains were not sustained at three months follow-up. The participant's ability and mobility may have increased following the intervention.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: Participants with PTHS may benefit from regular physical activity and early intervention. The Upsee mobility device is a feasible and fun way to promote inclusive community-based physical activity and social engagement in a young child with PTHS. Further research into the health benefits of physical activity and the Upsee for children with PTHS may be warranted. Implications for Rehabilitation Physical activity may be beneficial for a child with Pitt Hopkins syndrome, a rare genetic disorder. New design, implementation of mobility intervention for a child with neurodevelopmental disabilities. The Upsee mobility device may offer physical benefits for a child with a neurodevelopmental disability. The Upsee mobility device may offer social benefits for a child with a neurodevelopmental disability.
